To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the skin of the glabrous hand is densely innervated by two classes of rapidly and two classes of more slowly adapting mechanoreceptors, which are sensitive to forces applied normal or parallel to the skin; (2) the non-glabrous skin of the hand is also densely innervated, but the receptors are different, and the skin has hairs that are innervated by mechanoreceptors; (3) muscle is innervated by stretch and force sensitive mechan

the firing properties of single mechanoreceptors are determined by their structure (morphology) and the mechanical properties of their receptive fields, and that these properties are similar in the different tissues (skin, muscle, joints) in which they occur.

the mechanoreceptive aferents from the skin and joints are highly specialized to encode specific features of the mechanical stimuli they are designed to detect, such as the rate of change in force, direction of force, and the magnitude of force.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the physiological basis of sensation, particularly the role of mechanosensory nerve endings.
how single mechanoreceptors encode the mechanical properties of the skin, muscle and joints in the awake human.
the physiological and anatomical properties of low threshold mechanosensory receptors in the joints, muscles, periosteum and skin of the upper extremity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we know much about the mechanoreceptors of the skin, muscle and joint capsules, but little about those of the periosteum.
we do not know the sensory nerve endings that innervate bone and periosteum, and we do not know how these nerve endings signal.
we know much about the signalling capacity of mechanoreceptors, but much more remains to be discovered.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mechanoreceptors from all tissues studied encode forces applied to their receptive fields with remarkable fidelity.

the peripheral nervous system has evolved to encode the mechanical state of the body in a way that allows the central nervous system to interpret the state of the body and make appropriate adjustments.
mechanoreceptors are very sensitive and selective detectors of forces applied to or generated by the tissues in which they are embedded.
The main takeaway from our work is that

mechanoreceptor firing patterns are remarkably similar in the skin, muscles, and joints, and the similarities in firing patterns are not simply due to the fact that all of the afferents are myelinated and thus have a similar conduction velocity.
mechanoreceptors in different tissues have evolved to encode specific features of the stimuli to which they are most sensitive.

the firing of a single mechanoreceptor is a complex and dynamic process that is influenced by a variety of factors, such as the type of stimulus (e.g., ramp, step, sinusoidal, vibration), its direction, its velocity, and the force of the stimulus.
